claims.text: At fusion-relevant high temperatures, diffusion-mediated vacancy-assisted dislocation climb is the dominant mechanism governing high-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based and refractory alloys.
Diffusion-mediated vacancy-assisted dislocation climb is also the dominant mechanism governing toughness in tungsten-based and refractory alloys at high temperature.
Vacancy concentration and distribution near dislocation cores mediate the rate of dislocation climb.
Enhanced vacancy diffusion accelerates dislocation climb.
Dislocation climb provides a pathway for high-temperature plastic strain accommodation.
Dislocation climb increases toughness by reducing strain localization.
Increasing vacancy concentration while holding other microstructural features constant should increase the dislocation climb rate.
Increasing vacancy concentration should reduce flow stress and thereby signify enhanced plastic strain.
Increasing vacancy concentration should improve toughness relative to material with nominal vacancy levels.
Increased work-hardening capacity is an indicator of improved toughness in the proposed comparison.
The activation energy for deformation should align with vacancy migration energies if vacancy-mediated climb controls deformation.
Diffusion should be the primary deformation driver between approximately 1000 and 1500 °C at controlled fusion-relevant strain rates.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate at lower temperatures or when grain-boundary sliding becomes significant.
Atomistic simulations can be used to measure dislocation motion, stress-strain response, and deformation-related activation energies in the controlled comparison.
Varying only initial vacancy concentration between otherwise identical models isolates vacancy concentration as the tested cause.
